Vector databases store numerical representations of unstructured text data. When documents are ingested into the database, they are first segmented into chunks. The chunking strategy determines how much contextual information is retained within each individual unit. If chunks are too small, the surrounding semantic context is lost, making it difficult for the language model to understand the broader narrative. Conversely, if chunks are too large, the specific factual details become diluted within the excessive text, leading to lower similarity scores during nearest-neighbor search. In modern retrieval-augmented generation systems, finding the optimal balance between granularity and context retention is critical. Production systems typically evaluate both token and character counts to determine appropriate boundaries. Overlap between consecutive chunks helps bridge boundaries, ensuring that ideas split across chunks can still be matched by search queries. Ongoing evaluation ensures that changes to chunking parameters do not degrade downstream recall or precision.
